title: Month-over-month change

WITH m AS (
    SELECT DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(TransactionDate), MONTH(TransactionDate), 1) AS MonthStart,
           SUM(Amount) AS Total
    FROM banking.Transactions
    GROUP BY DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(TransactionDate), MONTH(TransactionDate), 1)

       LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY MonthStart)         AS PrevMonth,
       Total - LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY MonthStart) AS Change

title: Share of each status within its region
q: For each region and status, show the count and what percent it is of that region's transactions.

SELECT p.Region, e.Status, COUNT(*) AS Transactions,
       CAST(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY p.Region)
            AS decimal(5,1)) AS PctOfRegion
FROM banking.Transactions AS e
JOIN banking.Accounts AS p ON p.AccountID = e.AccountID
GROUP BY p.Region, e.Status
ORDER BY p.Region, Transactions DESC;

title: Accounts above their region's average
q: For each account, compare their total amount with the average account total in the same region. Show only accounts above their region's average.
sql:
WITH t AS (
    SELECT p.Region, e.AccountID, SUM(e.Amount) AS AccountTotal
    FROM banking.Transactions AS e
    JOIN banking.Accounts AS p ON p.AccountID = e.AccountID
    GROUP BY p.Region, e.AccountID
)
SELECT Region, AccountID, AccountTotal,
       CAST(RegionAvg AS decimal(10,2)) AS RegionAvg
FROM (SELECT *, AVG(AccountTotal) OVER (PARTITION BY Region) AS RegionAvg FROM t) AS x
WHERE AccountTotal > RegionAvg
ORDER BY Region, AccountTotal DESC;

title: Gaps and islands: busy-day streaks

WITH d AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT TransactionDate FROM banking.Transactions
), g AS (
    SELECT TransactionDate,
           DATEADD(day, -ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY TransactionDate), TransactionDate) AS grp

)

       MAX(TransactionDate) AS StreakEnd,
       COUNT(*)           AS Days
FROM g
GROUP BY grp

title: Repeat transactions within N days
q: Find transactions that happened within @Days days of the same account's previous transaction. Use @Days = 145. Show account, previous date, current date and gap.
sql:
DECLARE @Days int = 145;

WITH v AS (
    SELECT AccountID, TransactionID, TransactionDate,
           LAG(TransactionDate) OVER (PARTITION BY AccountID ORDER BY TransactionDate, TransactionID) AS PrevDate
    FROM banking.Transactions
)
SELECT AccountID, PrevDate, TransactionDate,
       DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, TransactionDate) AS GapDays
FROM v
WHERE PrevDate IS NOT NULL
  AND DATEDIFF(day, PrevDate, TransactionDate) <= @Days
ORDER BY AccountID, TransactionDate;
how: LAG finds the previous transaction and DATEDIFF measures the gap. A variable makes the window easy to change. Repeat-activity checks like this are a common interview question.

title: Transaction chain for one account
q: Starting from account 1's first transaction, use a recursive CTE to walk forward through that account's transactions in date order, with a step number.
sql:
WITH Ordered AS (
    SELECT TransactionID, TransactionDate,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY TransactionDate, TransactionID) AS rn
    FROM banking.Transactions
    WHERE AccountID = 1
), Chain AS (
    SELECT TransactionID, TransactionDate, rn, 0 AS Step
    FROM Ordered
    WHERE rn = 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.TransactionID, o.TransactionDate, o.rn, c.Step + 1
    FROM Ordered AS o
    JOIN Chain AS c ON o.rn = c.rn + 1
)
SELECT TransactionID, TransactionDate, Step
FROM Chain
ORDER BY Step;

title: MAXRECURSION
q: Generate numbers 1 to 200 with a recursive CTE. (The default limit is 100 levels.)
sql:
WITH N AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM N WHERE n < 200
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS HowMany, MAX(n) AS LastNumber
FROM N
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 200);
how: SQL Server stops recursion after 100 levels by default. OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) raises the limit; 0 means no limit, which is risky.

title: Month-over-month with a calendar
q: For all 12 months of 2024 (even empty ones), show total amount, previous month's total and growth %.
sql:
WITH Months AS (
    SELECT CAST('2024-01-01' AS date) AS m
    UNION ALL
    SELECT DATEADD(month, 1, m) FROM Months WHERE m < '2024-12-01'
), Totals AS (
    SELECT mo.m, ISNULL(SUM(e.Amount), 0) AS Total
    FROM Months AS mo
    LEFT JOIN banking.Transactions AS e
           ON e.TransactionDate >= mo.m AND e.TransactionDate < DATEADD(month, 1, mo.m)
    GROUP BY mo.m
)
SELECT m AS MonthStart, Total,
       LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m) AS PrevTotal,
       CAST(100.0 * (Total - LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m))
            / NULLIF(LAG(Total) OVER (ORDER BY m), 0) AS decimal(6,1)) AS GrowthPct
FROM Totals
ORDER BY m;

title: Org-chart style hierarchy with path
q: Build a small hierarchy in a table variable (region head > team > account) and list it with a recursive CTE, showing each level and a path like Head > North > Olivia.
sql:
DECLARE @Org TABLE (NodeID int, ParentID int NULL, NodeName nvarchar(100));
INSERT INTO @Org VALUES (0, NULL, N'Head');
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Region), 0, Region
FROM banking.Accounts
GROUP BY Region;
INSERT INTO @Org
SELECT 100 + p.AccountID, r.NodeID, p.AccountName
FROM banking.Accounts AS p
JOIN @Org AS r ON r.NodeName = p.Region
WHERE p.AccountID <= 6;

WITH Tree AS (
    SELECT NodeID, NodeName, 0 AS Lvl, CAST(NodeName AS nvarchar(400)) AS PathText
    FROM @Org
    WHERE ParentID IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.NodeID, o.NodeName, t.Lvl + 1,
           CAST(t.PathText + N' > ' + o.NodeName AS nvarchar(400))
    FROM @Org AS o
    JOIN Tree AS t ON o.ParentID = t.NodeID
)
SELECT NodeID, Lvl, PathText
FROM Tree
ORDER BY PathText;

title: MERGE: sync a staging table
q: Sync account regions from a staging list: update regions that changed, insert new accounts, and report each action.
sql:
DECLARE @Stage TABLE (AccountID int, AccountName nvarchar(80), AccountNumber varchar(20), Region varchar(10));
INSERT INTO @Stage
SELECT AccountID, AccountName, AccountNumber, CASE WHEN Region = 'East' THEN 'West' ELSE 'East' END
FROM banking.Accounts WHERE AccountID = 1          -- region change
UNION ALL
SELECT AccountID, AccountName, AccountNumber, Region
FROM banking.Accounts WHERE AccountID = 2          -- no change
UNION ALL
SELECT 301, N'New Account', '71020000000301', 'North';     -- new

MERGE banking.Accounts AS t
USING @Stage AS s
   ON t.AccountID = s.AccountID
WHEN MATCHED AND t.Region <> s.Region THEN
    UPDATE SET t.Region = s.Region
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (AccountID, AccountName, AccountNumber, Region, CustomerID, BranchID)
    VALUES (s.AccountID, s.AccountName, s.AccountNumber, s.Region, 1, 1)
OUTPUT $action AS ActionTaken, inserted.AccountID, deleted.Region AS OldRegion, inserted.Region AS NewRegion;
how: MERGE does insert, update and (optionally) delete in one statement. The extra `AND t.Region <> s.Region` skips rows that did not change. $action in OUTPUT reports what happened to each row.

title: Isolation levels
q: Name SQL Server's transaction isolation levels and the problem each one prevents. Show the current level.
sql:
SELECT CASE transaction_isolation_level
         WHEN 1 THEN 'READ UNCOMMITTED' WHEN 2 THEN 'READ COMMITTED'
         WHEN 3 THEN 'REPEATABLE READ'  WHEN 4 THEN 'SERIALIZABLE'
         WHEN 5 THEN 'SNAPSHOT' END AS IsolationLevel
FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions
WHERE session_id = @@SPID;
how: READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads. READ COMMITTED (the default) prevents dirty reads. REPEATABLE READ also prevents non-repeatable reads. SERIALIZABLE also prevents phantom rows. SNAPSHOT reads a consistent version without blocking writers. Higher isolation means fewer anomalies but more blocking.

title: Self join: next transaction
q: Pair each transaction with the same account's next transaction. Show both IDs and dates.

WITH n AS (
    SELECT TransactionID, AccountID, TransactionDate,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY AccountID ORDER BY TransactionDate, TransactionID) AS rn
    FROM banking.Transactions
)
SELECT a.AccountID, a.TransactionID, a.TransactionDate,
       b.TransactionID AS NextID, b.TransactionDate AS NextDate
FROM n AS a
JOIN n AS b ON b.AccountID = a.AccountID AND b.rn = a.rn + 1
ORDER BY a.AccountID, a.TransactionDate;

title: Joins that multiply rows
q: Show each account's total transaction amount and number of Open transactions. Make sure the amount is not double counted.
sql:
SELECT p.AccountID, p.AccountName,
       ISNULL(ch.TotalAmount, 0) AS TotalAmount,
       ISNULL(op.OpenTransactions, 0) AS OpenTransactions
FROM banking.Accounts AS p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT AccountID, SUM(Amount) AS TotalAmount
           FROM banking.Transactions
           GROUP BY AccountID) AS ch ON ch.AccountID = p.AccountID
LEFT JOIN (SELECT AccountID, COUNT(*) AS OpenTransactions
           FROM banking.Transactions
           WHERE Status = 'Open'
           GROUP BY AccountID) AS op ON op.AccountID = p.AccountID
ORDER BY TotalAmount DESC, p.AccountID;
how: Joining two child row sets and then summing makes each amount count once per matching row (fan-out). Aggregating each set separately before joining fixes this. Interviewers often test whether you spot fan-out.

title: EXCEPT vs NOT EXISTS with duplicates

SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT AccountID FROM banking.Transactions
                         EXCEPT
                         SELECT AccountID FROM banking.Transactions WHERE Status = 'Pending') AS x) AS ExceptRows,

   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM banking.Transactions AS e2
                     WHERE e2.AccountID = e.AccountID AND e2.Status = 'Pending')) AS NotExistsRows;

title: NOT IN and the NULL trap
q: Interview trap: show why NOT IN fails when the list contains NULL. Find transactions that are not a parent of any other transaction, first with NOT IN (wrong), then with NOT EXISTS (right).
sql:
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM banking.Transactions AS e
   WHERE e.TransactionID NOT IN (SELECT ParentTransactionID
                               FROM banking.Transactions)) AS NotIn_Wrong,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM banking.Transactions AS e
   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM banking.Transactions AS c
                     WHERE c.ParentTransactionID = e.TransactionID)) AS NotExists_Right;
how: ParentTransactionID is NULL on every row here. `x NOT IN (..., NULL)` is never true, so NOT IN returns 0. NOT EXISTS ignores the NULLs and correctly finds that no transaction is a parent. You can also fix NOT IN by adding `WHERE ParentTransactionID IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery.
